offence_severity: Death caused by explosive substance (Section 302 IPC) with life imprisonment as maximum punishment
physical_harm: Deceased succumbed to injuries caused by explosive substance; other witnesses suffered injuries in the occurrence
number_of_offences: Multiple offences charged under Sections 302, 323, 324, 149, and 148 IPC; High Court upheld convictions for all accused
premeditation_planning: The court found that Mangal Singh threw the bomb with pre-determined mind
motive: Assault and hurling of abuses in filthy language
key_evidence_accepted: The prosecution established the presence and active participation of the appellant as a member of the unlawful assembly, and the deceased's death was homicidal in nature caused by an explosive substance. The witnesses were reliable, and their testimony was supported by medical evidence and the FIR.
witness_credibility: The witnesses were found to be reliable, with their testimony supported by medical evidence and the FIR. Their injuries sustained during the incident were considered to enhance their credibility, as they were present at the scene and their accounts were consistent.

legal_representation.accused: Varinder Kumar Sharma, Vipin Kumar, K. K. Shrivastava (for Deepak Goel)

investigation_status: FIR registered, charge sheet filed, trial completed
prosecution_argument: The prosecution argued that the accused persons formed an unlawful assembly with a common object to assault the deceased, who succumbed to the injuries inflicted. The prosecution established the presence and active participation of the appellant as a member of the unlawful assembly, and that the accused were the aggressors who hurled abuses and threw bombs at the deceased.
defence_argument: The defence argued that the trial court's acquittal was plausible and that the High Court should not have reversed it. They contended that the prosecution failed to explain why other witnesses were not examined and that the appellant should not be convicted under Section 302 IPC as he did not directly assault the deceased.
legal_principle_applied: The Supreme Court applied the principle that the punishment under Section 149 IPC is vicarious and does not require each member of the unlawful assembly to commit an overt act. The court emphasized that mere presence in an unlawful assembly can make one liable if the common object of the assembly is to commit an offence.
precedent_relied_upon: Gamini Bala Koteswara Rao v. State of A.P. (2009) 10 SCC 636; Kallu v. State of M.P. (2006) 10 SCC 313; Ramesh Babula! Doshi v. State of Gujarat (1996) 9 SCC 225; Ganpat v. State of Haryana (2010) 12 SCC 59; State of Punjab v. Kamai Singh (2003) 11 SCC 271; Jugendra Singh v. State of Uttar Pradesh (2012) 6 SCC 297; Basappa v. State of Karnataka (2014) 5 SCC 154
sentencing_rationale: The final sentence was imposed because the High Court found that the accused persons were aggressors who formed an unlawful assembly with a common object to assault the deceased, and the prosecution's version was credible and supported by evidence, including the testimony of injured witnesses.
